templates.description: The core recovery-test loop for a snapshot/point-in-time recovery tool: launch the environment in the recovery region from aligned recovery points, verify layer by layer, prove a business transaction, then triage everything you learned.
templates.whenToUse: Use for every Phase-1 recovery test with a snapshot-recovery tool (Arpio or similar). No DNS is touched and no live traffic moves — the success bar is a business transaction against the recovered stack via direct endpoints.
templates.name: Recovery test — snapshot recovery (Arpio-style)
preconditions: Phase 0 checklist is green and signed off
Recovery scope re-selected and saved in the recovery tool within the last week
Operator and approver both on the calendar for the full window
Agreed T0 definition written in the test plan (T0 = recovery launch initiated)
NETWORK ISOLATION DECISION recorded for this test: sandbox ON is the default; disabling it requires the named approver acknowledgement in the network-isolation step
VPC endpoints for ECR (api + dkr), S3, Secrets Manager, STS, KMS and CloudWatch Logs exist in the recovery VPC — this is what lets the drill run with the sandbox ON

steps.title: Pre-flight: record T0 and recovery-point alignment
steps.detail: Open the test record. Write the wall-clock T0 the moment you initiate recovery. In the recovery tool, confirm the recovery points for ALL protected resources are aligned to the same point-in-time set (databases, S3, SQS, ECR from the same sync). Screenshot the recovery-point list — this is your RPA evidence.
steps.command: arpio recovery-points list --environment <env> # placeholder
steps.verify: Every in-scope resource shows a recovery point within the configured RPO window, all from the same sync set
steps.pass: Aligned recovery points, none older than RPO target; screenshot saved
steps.record: T0 timestamp; recovery-point ages per resource (this is RPA at T0)

steps.title: Pre-flight: network isolation ON (and what it takes to justify turning it off)
steps.detail:
DEFAULT: the network sandbox / isolated networking is **ON**, and the production-touch guards are ON. This is a correction of earlier guidance in this template, which told operators to turn the sandbox OFF. The sandbox is the control that blocks outbound internet from the recovered test environment — it is what stops a drill emailing real customers, POSTing real claims to the partner clearinghouse, uploading real settlement files over SFTP, firing real webhooks, or calling a payment provider. A recovered environment is a faithful copy of production, including its credentials and its endpoints: with egress open it will do production things. Losing a test window is recoverable; sending a drill claim to a real partner is not.

WHY PEOPLE TURN IT OFF, AND WHY THEY DO NOT NEED TO. The usual reason is that image pulls and secrets resolution appear to need internet egress. They do not. Both are reachable with zero internet egress through VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink), and this is the safer fix:
  - com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.api and com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.dkr (interface) — registry API and image push/pull
  - com.amazonaws.<region>.s3 (GATEWAY endpoint) — REQUIRED alongside the ECR endpoints, because ECR stores image layers in S3; without it pulls fail after the manifest is fetched, which looks exactly like a mysterious network problem
  - com.amazonaws.<region>.secretsmanager (interface) — secret retrieval
  - com.amazonaws.<region>.sts (interface) — note that the STS GLOBAL endpoint bypasses the VPC endpoint, so the workload must be configured to use the REGIONAL STS endpoint or IRSA will still try to leave the VPC
  - com.amazonaws.<region>.kms (interface) — needed when secrets or volumes use customer-managed keys
  - com.amazonaws.<region>.logs (interface) — if anything ships logs via the awslogs driver
Caveat worth knowing: ECR pull-through cache rules need an internet path on the first pull of an image, so pre-pull or replicate those images into your own repositories instead of relying on the cache during a drill.

OTHER SAFE ALTERNATIVE: pre-pull the images into the recovery-region registry (or use native ECR cross-region replication) before the window, so nothing needs to fetch anything.

IF THE SANDBOX MUST BE OFF. Only as a deliberate, time-boxed exception, and only with this acknowledgement recorded verbatim in the test record, signed by the named approver: "I acknowledge the network sandbox is OFF for this drill. The recovered environment can reach real third parties. I have verified that outbound webhooks, schedulers and batch jobs are disabled and that no production data-plane endpoint is reachable from the recovered environment." Then prove it, do not assert it — the verification below is the proof, and a missing acknowledgement is a stop.
steps.command:
arpio environment show <env> --settings # placeholder: confirm sandbox/isolation = ON
# IF THE SANDBOX IS OFF, prove the blast radius is contained FROM INSIDE the recovered
# environment. Use whichever probe the image supports; if it has neither curl nor nc,
# run the same loop in a debug pod on the SAME node/subnet and security group.
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> exec deploy/<tier0-app> -- sh -c '
  for ep in <partner-clearinghouse-host> <settlement-sftp-host> <payment-provider-host> <prod-db-host>; do
    if curl -s -o /dev/null --max-time 5 "https://$ep" 2>/dev/null; then echo "REACHABLE: $ep";
    elif command -v nc >/dev/null && nc -z -w 5 "$ep" 443 2>/dev/null; then echo "REACHABLE: $ep";
    else echo "blocked: $ep"; fi
  done'
# Confirm nothing is scheduled to fire outward on its own:
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get cronjobs -A -o wide   # every outbound job must be SUSPEND=true
aws lambda list-event-source-mappings --region <recovery-region> --query "EventSourceMappings[?State=='Enabled'].[UUID,FunctionArn]" --output table   # expect empty
steps.verify: Sandbox/isolation = ON and flags match the test plan. IF OFF: zero "REACHABLE:" lines across every production and third-party data-plane endpoint on the list (and the probe demonstrably ran — a probe that silently found no curl/nc proves nothing); every outbound cronjob shows SUSPEND=true; the enabled-event-source-mapping list is empty; the verbatim acknowledgement is in the record with the approver's name
steps.pass: Sandbox ON (normal case) — OR sandbox OFF with the acknowledgement recorded AND containment verified from inside the recovered environment, not asserted. No acknowledgement, or any reachable partner/production endpoint, = do not launch.
steps.record: Flag values as launched; sandbox ON/OFF; if OFF: the acknowledgement text, the approver, the containment probe output, and the list of endpoints tested

steps.title: Launch ops/shared-services account first
steps.detail: Start recovery of the ops account (ECR registries, shared tooling) BEFORE the app account. App pods cannot start until their images exist in the recovery-region registry — ordering is not optional.
steps.command: arpio recover start --environment <ops-env> # placeholder
steps.verify: Recovery job for ops account running; ECR repositories appearing in recovery region
steps.pass: All ECR repositories present with expected image tags
steps.record: Ops launch start/finish times

steps.title: Launch application account
steps.detail: Start recovery of the application environment (VPC, EKS, databases, queues, buckets, secrets) from the aligned recovery points. Note the exact start time — cold-start duration is a number leadership will ask for.
steps.command: arpio recover start --environment <app-env> # placeholder
steps.verify: Recovery job running; resources appearing in the recovery region in dependency order
steps.pass: Recovery job reports complete with zero failed resources
steps.record: App launch start/finish; any resources the tool reported as failed or skipped

steps.title: Verify platform: nodes, mesh, DNS, controllers
steps.detail: The cluster exists — now prove it is a platform. Nodes Ready, CoreDNS resolving, service mesh control plane up, load-balancer controller and autoscaler running. Do not look at app pods yet; a broken platform makes every app failure a red herring.
steps.command: kubectl get nodes && kubectl get pods -n kube-system && kubectl get pods -n istio-system
steps.verify: All nodes Ready; CoreDNS, istiod, ALB controller, Karpenter all Running
steps.pass: Platform pods healthy, no CrashLoopBackOff in system namespaces
steps.record: Node count, any system pods restarted manually

steps.title: Verify data layer: databases and queues restored
steps.detail: Connect to each restored database from inside the recovery VPC and run a freshness query (latest transaction timestamp). Compare against T0 — the difference is your measured RPA. Confirm queues exist; accept documented in-flight message loss.
steps.command: psql -h <recovered-endpoint> -c "SELECT max(updated_at) FROM <hot-table>" # placeholder
steps.verify: Every database answers; latest-row timestamps within the recovery-point window
steps.pass: All databases reachable and fresh; RPA per database recorded
steps.record: Measured RPA (data age at T0) per database

steps.title: Verify secrets: the APPLICATION can obtain and use every secret (tests usually die HERE)
steps.detail:
This is the layer where recovery tests most often fail, and it is worth being precise about what counts as proof — because the check this template used to recommend did not prove anything useful.

WHY describe-secret IS NOT ENOUGH. `aws secretsmanager describe-secret` returns METADATA ONLY — the AWS API reference says plainly "It does not include the encrypted secret value", and there is no SecretString field in its response at all. It therefore succeeds when the replica exists with no usable value, when the KMS key is missing or its policy does not allow you, and when the APPLICATION'S role has no permission (you ran it as an admin). Verified 2026-09-16: DescribeSecret is absent from the list of Secrets Manager operations that require AWS KMS permissions, so it never exercises a decrypt. It is a shape check masquerading as a bytes check.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD — three things, in this order:
1. RECONCILIATION DIFF: needed (the signed-off list) vs present-in-recovery. Zero missing, zero staler than RPO.
2. DECRYPT PROBE: `get-secret-value` returns the plaintext and therefore FORCES a KMS Decrypt against the encrypting key — AWS documents GetSecretValue as one of the operations that require kms:Decrypt. Run it once per KMS key in play. This is the check that catches "perfectly replicated ciphertext nobody can decrypt", which is a very durable form of data loss.
3. APP-IDENTITY PROBE — the one that matters most: run get-secret-value from the WORKLOAD'S OWN IDENTITY, not an admin's. An admin read proves the secret exists; only the application's role proves the IAM plumbing (role policies, resource policies, and the OIDC trust of a recovered EKS cluster whose issuer URL is DIFFERENT from the primary's) also made the trip. A recovered or second cluster has a new OIDC issuer, so every IRSA trust policy must already trust it or every pod silently loses its AWS identity.
Also confirm the app's startup probe / secrets-init actually passes with those secrets, and check the ROTATION FREEZE: no rotation lambda is due to fire mid-recovery, and any that can are disabled or region-aware.

If you have nothing but admin credentials to hand, say so in the record and raise it as a finding — do not record an admin read as if it were an app-identity read.
steps.command:
# Preferred: exec into the REAL workload — it already runs as the tier-0 identity.
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> exec deploy/<tier0-app> -- sh -c 'aws sts get-caller-identity && aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id <one-tier0-secret> --region <recovery-region> --query SecretString --output text >/dev/null && echo ok'
# Full sweep (use when the app image has no AWS CLI): mount the signed-off list into a
# probe pod bound to the SAME ServiceAccount, so the IRSA identity is identical.
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> create configmap dr-secret-list --from-file=signed-off-secrets.txt --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> apply -f -
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> run secret-probe --rm -i --restart=Never --image <recovery-registry>/aws-cli:<tag> --overrides='{"spec":{"serviceAccountName":"<tier0-serviceaccount>","containers":[{"name":"secret-probe","image":"<recovery-registry>/aws-cli:<tag>","volumeMounts":[{"name":"l","mountPath":"/l"}],"command":["sh","-c","aws sts get-caller-identity; while read s; do aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id \"$s\" --region <recovery-region> --query SecretString --output text >/dev/null && echo \"ok: $s\" || echo \"FAIL: $s\"; done </l/signed-off-secrets.txt"]}],"volumes":[{"name":"l","configMap":{"name":"dr-secret-list"}}]}}'
# Last resort if neither is possible: the app's own startup probe / secrets-init must pass.
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> logs -l app=<tier0-app> -c secrets-init --tail=50 | grep -iE 'error|notfound|accessdenied' && echo "SECRETS FAILING" || echo "secrets-init clean"
# Reconciliation diff — what is needed vs what is actually in the recovery region:
aws secretsmanager list-secrets --region <recovery-region> --query "SecretList[].Name" --output text | tr "\t" "\n" | sort > present.txt
sort signed-off-secrets.txt > needed.txt && comm -23 needed.txt present.txt   # ANY output = MISSING
# Rotation freeze — nothing may rotate inside the window:
aws secretsmanager list-secrets --region <recovery-region> --query "SecretList[?RotationEnabled].[Name,NextRotationDate]" --output table
steps.verify: comm output empty (nothing needed-but-absent); zero FAIL lines from the app-identity probe; sts get-caller-identity returns the tier-0 IRSA ROLE (not the node instance role, not an admin); at least one get-secret-value per KMS key in play returned a value; secrets-init / startup probe logs clean; no rotation due inside the window
steps.pass: Every signed-off secret retrieved BY THE APPLICATION IDENTITY (this proves existence + KMS decrypt + IAM/OIDC trust in one command) and the app's own startup probe passes. Any FAIL line, or a caller identity that is not the app role, is a blocker finding — stop here rather than starting apps and debugging L4 symptoms of an L3 cause.
steps.record: Caller identity returned by the probe; any missing or failing secret (immediate blocker finding); KMS key ids exercised; rotation-freeze confirmation

steps.title: Verify applications: pods up, images from recovery registry
steps.detail: Scale up / confirm app workloads. Check that pods are Running AND that their image references point at the RECOVERY-region registry, not the primary one (a pod pulling cross-region from the dead primary is a silent lie in a real event).
steps.command: kubectl get deploy -A && kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[0].image}{"\n"}{end}' | sort -u
steps.verify: All Tier-0/1 deployments Ready; every image host is the recovery-region registry
steps.pass: Apps Ready; zero images referencing the primary region
steps.record: Time from launch to all apps Ready (cold-start number)

steps.title: Verify edge WITHOUT touching DNS
steps.detail: Prove reachability through the recovered API Gateway / load balancer using the DIRECT endpoint with a Host header matching the real domain. Public DNS is never changed in Phase 1 — the point is to prove the edge would work if it were.
steps.command: curl -sk https://<recovery-execute-api-endpoint>/api/switch/healthcheck -H 'Host: api.<your-domain>'
steps.verify: HTTP 200 from the recovery edge; response comes from recovered backends
steps.pass: Healthcheck 200 with backend detail via direct endpoint + Host header
steps.record: Endpoint used, response body snippet

steps.title: Functional success bar: business transaction end-to-end
steps.detail: Run the agreed business transaction against the recovered stack (e.g. submit a test claim through the API and receive a real business response, not a 500). This — not green pods — is what 'recovered' means. Note the wall-clock time: first successful business transaction = T1.
steps.command: curl -sk -X POST https://<recovery-endpoint>/<business-tx-path> -H 'Host: api.<your-domain>' -d @test-transaction.json
steps.verify: Business-level success response with a real transaction id
steps.pass: Transaction answered end-to-end; T1 recorded; RTA = T1 − T0
steps.record: T1 timestamp; computed RTA in minutes

steps.title: Functional success bar: settlement/back-office path
steps.detail: Prove the second half of the bar: the settlement or batch path (e.g. remittance import runs against the recovered bucket/queue and writes to the recovered database). Front-door success with a dead settlement path is still an outage for finance.
steps.command: kubectl -n <ns> create job --from=cronjob/<settlement-import> test-import && kubectl logs job/test-import -f
steps.verify: Import job completes; rows land in the recovered database
steps.pass: Settlement path runs clean end-to-end
steps.record: Job result; row counts

steps.title: Conclude: no failback without explicit approval
steps.detail: The test environment is torn down / recovery concluded ONLY on the approver's explicit go. Never trigger the tool's failback/teardown reflexively — in some tools failback has production side effects. Record who approved and when.
steps.verify: Written approval (chat message or ticket) from the named approver
steps.pass: Approval captured, then teardown executed
steps.record: Approver name, approval timestamp, teardown time

steps.title: Triage findings same-day: gaps, tickets, runbook edits
steps.detail: While it hurts, write the record: every surprise becomes (a) a gap with severity, (b) a ticket, or (c) an edit to this runbook — usually all three. A finding that lives only in someone's head is a finding you will rediscover during the real event.
steps.verify: Every finding in the test record has a gap id or ticket id next to it
steps.pass: Test record written same day; findings filed; runbook updated
steps.record: Findings list with severities and destinations

rollback.title: Tear down the recovered test environment
rollback.detail: After approval, conclude the recovery in the tool so test resources are destroyed and replication resumes toward the recovery region. Verify replication returns to green.
rollback.verify: Recovery-region test resources gone; replication status green again
rollback.pass: Tool shows protected + replicating; no orphaned resources billing in the recovery region
rollback.record: Teardown complete time; replication green time

templates.notes: Phase 1 never touches public DNS or live traffic. RTA/RPA measured here are the only honest numbers until a game day. Two safety defaults corrected in this template: the network sandbox stays ON (the network-isolation step — it is what stops a drill calling real partners; VPC endpoints, not open egress, are the answer to image pulls and secrets), and the L3 secrets gate proves the APPLICATION can obtain and decrypt each secret (the L3 secrets step — describe-secret returns metadata only and proves none of that). Sources: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/apireference/API_DescribeSecret.html , https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/security-encryption.html , https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/vpc-endpoints.html , https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/vpc-endpoint-overview.html , https://docs.arpio.io/network-sandbox . Estimated minutes are a planning estimate, not a schedule.

templates.templateName: AWS Region switch — planned switchover OR unplanned failover
templates.description: Failover orchestrated by an ARC Region switch plan, split into two explicitly different paths: a PLANNED SWITCHOVER (graceful mode, both regions healthy, zero data loss expected) and an UNPLANNED FAILOVER (ungraceful mode, primary unreachable or degraded, data loss possible). Fences the old primary before any promotion, gates secrets and image provenance before apps, and proves a business transaction in the recovery region BEFORE any live traffic moves.
templates.whenToUse: Use when AWS ARC Region switch (or a comparable orchestrator) owns the failover sequence. Requires the plan to already exist in BOTH regions and to have been executed at least once in graceful mode against a lower environment in the last quarter — a plan first run during a disaster is a hypothesis, not a plan. There is NO practice or simulation mode for Region switch: rehearsal means a real graceful execution. The PATH DECISION step chooses which of the two paths below you are on; do not start the plan before it is chosen, approved and recorded.
templates.name: Regional switchover / failover — Region switch plan
preconditions: PATH DECIDED FIRST: planned switchover (graceful) or unplanned failover (ungraceful) — see the PATH DECISION step. Every precondition below is annotated with which path it applies to.
BOTH PATHS — Region switch plan exists and is healthy in BOTH regions (you trigger from the one you are activating)

BOTH PATHS — the plan has been executed end to end in GRACEFUL mode against a lower environment within the last quarter, and the plan version has not changed since (there is no practice mode; an un-exercised plan edit is a reason to pause)
BOTH PATHS — the plan contains a Manual approval execution block before the data promotion and another before the traffic block; without them you cannot gate an execution once it starts
BOTH PATHS — plan evaluation status has no unacknowledged warnings (evaluation runs every ~30 min; AWS states it is NOT a substitute for executing the plan)
BOTH PATHS — execution role permissions verified in the recovery region, and the operator can authenticate to the recovery account WITHOUT the primary region or primary-region SSO
BOTH PATHS — named decision-maker reachable for the approval gates, and a rollback owner named
BOTH PATHS — secrets reconciled to ONE signed-off list and verified resolvable by the APPLICATION identity in the recovery region (the secrets gate)
BOTH PATHS — recovery-region images present in the recovery-region registry, and recovery-region quota/capacity headroom confirmed for the scale-up

SWITCHOVER ONLY — both regions healthy, replication lag near zero, and a change/maintenance window agreed. Aurora Global switchover requires a healthy primary; if the primary is impaired, switchover is not available to you and you are on the failover path.
SWITCHOVER ONLY — writers in the old region can be quiesced cleanly (maintenance mode / scale to zero) so no writes are in flight across the cut
FAILOVER ONLY — the primary is declared unreachable or unacceptably degraded by the incident commander, and the declaration is recorded
FAILOVER ONLY — the accepted data-loss window has been stated in writing before execution (it equals the replication lag at the moment of failure, and it is not zero)
FAILOVER ONLY — a reconciliation owner is named for writes that were accepted in the old region and not replicated

steps.title: Confirm plan health and trigger region
steps.detail: Check the plan in the RECOVERY region (assume the primary region console and its APIs are unavailable — that is the whole point of the per-region data plane). Confirm the plan version is the version you last exercised. Region switch plan configuration lives in a us-east-1 control plane, but execution, cancel and update are data-plane operations with an independent endpoint and console in each region, so you execute from the region you are ACTIVATING.
steps.command: aws arc-region-switch get-plan-in-region --plan-arn <plan-arn> --region <recovery-region> && aws arc-region-switch get-plan-evaluation-status --plan-arn <plan-arn> --region <recovery-region>
steps.verify: Plan returned from the recovery-region endpoint; evaluation status has no unacknowledged warnings; plan version equals the version recorded in the last graceful exercise
steps.pass: Plan healthy AND readable from the recovery region AND version matches the last exercised version (a mismatch is a HOLD, not a warning)
steps.record: Plan version, evaluation status, which region you read it from

steps.title: DECIDE THE PATH: planned switchover (graceful) or unplanned failover (ungraceful)
steps.detail: These are different operations with different data outcomes and different rollback stories, and the runbook has been split so you cannot drift between them. GRACEFUL = planned switchover: every block takes its safe path, the Aurora Global Database block performs a SWITCHOVER (Aurora syncs the secondary before changing anything, so RPO is 0 and the old writer is demoted for you), and it requires a healthy primary. UNGRACEFUL = unplanned failover: blocks take the lossy-but-fast path, the Aurora block performs a FAILOVER (data not yet replicated is LOST, RPO = replication lag at failure), some blocks are changed and some are SKIPPED ENTIRELY (custom Lambda actions and Lambda event-source-mapping blocks among them — check your plan), and the old writer is NOT demoted for you, which is why the FENCE step exists. Write down which path, why, who decided, and for the failover path the expected loss window in seconds. If the primary is healthy and you have a window, you are on the switchover path; choosing ungraceful for convenience throws away RPO 0 for nothing.
steps.verify: Path and mode written in the incident/test record with the decider, the reason, and (failover path) the current replication lag captured as the expected loss window
steps.pass: One path chosen, in writing, before the plan is started — and the operator can state the data consequence of that choice out loud
steps.record: graceful|ungraceful; decider; reason; expected data-loss window (seconds) and the metric it came from

steps.title: APPROVAL GATE: authorize execution on the chosen path
steps.detail: Real execution moves data primaries and, later, public traffic. The named decision-maker approves in writing. For the failover path the approval explicitly acknowledges the data-loss window from the PATH DECISION step and names the reconciliation owner. Record the business reason and the incident id. This timestamp is T0 for the RTA measurement.
steps.verify: Written approval captured; incident ticket open; for the failover path the approval text contains the accepted loss window and the reconciliation owner
steps.pass: Approval logged with timestamp, path, and accepted data-loss window
steps.record: Approver, timestamp, incident id, path — this is T0

steps.title: FENCE THE OLD PRIMARY before any promotion (split-brain gate)
steps.detail:
Do this BEFORE the data block runs, on both paths. Split-brain is the one failure worse than downtime: two writers on a claims ledger is unrecoverable in a way that an outage is not, and the realistic regional event is a GRAY failure, not a clean crater — the old region keeps answering some clients, especially those whose DNS has not moved. Note that an Aurora Global SWITCHOVER demotes the old writer for you but an UNGRACEFUL FAILOVER does NOT.

SWITCHOVER path (primary reachable): quiesce, do not amputate. Put the old region into maintenance mode or scale its writer workloads to zero, disable its schedulers/cron/batch and its Lambda event source mappings, let in-flight transactions drain, and confirm the old writer has zero application connections. Then the switchover cuts with nothing in flight.

FAILOVER path (primary unreachable or degraded): fence whatever you can still reach, in this order — (1) revoke the old writer's database security-group ingress; (2) scale old-region workloads to zero; (3) disable old-region schedulers and event source mappings; (4) take the OLD region's edge out of service (disable its health check target / set its listener to a failure response) so clients holding stale DNS cannot keep writing there. Fencing the edge matters as much as fencing the database.

If you cannot reach the old region at all, you cannot fence it. That is a legitimate state — record it POSITIVELY ("could not fence: old region unreachable at HH:MM, split-brain risk accepted, reconciliation owner X") rather than leaving it blank. Do not invent reachability you do not have, and do not delay a declared failover waiting for a fence you cannot apply.
steps.command:
# switchover path (old region reachable):
kubectl --context <primary-ctx> -n <ns> scale deploy --all --replicas=0 && aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier <old-writer> --region <primary-region> --query "DBClusters[0].DBClusterMembers"
# then confirm connections have drained (Aurora PostgreSQL):
psql -h <old-writer-endpoint> -c "SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state IS NOT NULL AND application_name NOT LIKE 'psql%'"
# failover path (old region degraded) — revoke DB ingress and disable schedulers:
aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress --group-id <db-sg> --protocol tcp --port 5432 --source-group <app-sg> --region <primary-region>
aws lambda list-event-source-mappings --region <primary-region> --query "EventSourceMappings[?State=='Enabled'].UUID" --output text | xargs -n1 -I{} aws lambda update-event-source-mapping --uuid {} --no-enabled --region <primary-region>
steps.verify: Application connections to the old writer are ZERO (or the old region is provably unreachable); old-region schedulers and event source mappings disabled; old-region edge no longer accepting writes
steps.pass: Old primary fenced with evidence (connection count zero / ingress revoked / edge out of service) — OR unreachability recorded explicitly with the split-brain risk accepted in writing and a named reconciliation owner. A blank record is a FAIL.
steps.record: Fencing method(s) used per resource, evidence for each, timestamp, and anything you could NOT fence

steps.title: Start plan execution in the chosen mode
steps.detail: Start the execution from the region you are ACTIVATING. Two separate parameters matter and they are often confused: --action says which direction (activate the target region / deactivate it / run a post-recovery workflow) and --mode says graceful or ungraceful. Verified 2026-09-16 against the AWS CLI and API references: the valid --mode values are exactly "graceful" and "ungraceful", lowercase; --mode is optional and defaults to graceful; --action is REQUIRED with values activate | deactivate | postRecovery; --plan-arn and --target-region are also required. There is no "failover" mode value and no practice mode. Note the execution id — everything after this is monitored through the execution and its report, and the abort path is cancel-plan-execution.
steps.command:
aws arc-region-switch start-plan-execution \
  --plan-arn <plan-arn> \
  --target-region <recovery-region> \
  --action activate \
  --mode <graceful|ungraceful> \
  --comment "<incident id> path=<switchover|failover> approver=<name>" \
  --region <recovery-region>
# abort path, if you need it: aws arc-region-switch cancel-plan-execution --plan-arn <plan-arn> --execution-id <id> --region <recovery-region>
steps.verify: Execution started; executionId returned; the mode in the execution matches the mode approved in the PATH DECISION step
steps.pass: Execution visible and progressing from the recovery-region endpoint, in the approved mode (if the mode is wrong, cancel and restart — do not "carry on and watch")
steps.record: Execution id, start time, mode and action as actually submitted

steps.title: Block: data switchover / failover — verify the new writer and the loss window
steps.detail: The plan's database block promotes the recovery-region cluster. Which operation it performs is decided by the mode you chose in the PATH DECISION step, and the difference is the whole point: graceful = SWITCHOVER, AWS syncs the secondary before making any other change, RPO 0, requires a healthy primary; ungraceful = FAILOVER, a non-zero RPO measured in seconds equal to the replication lag at failure, and no demotion of the old writer. Confirm the writer endpoint is now in the recovery region, that the cluster ACCEPTS A WRITE (not merely that it reports "available"), and measure the actual data staleness — that number is your RPA and it goes in the record whichever path you took. Create the dr_write_probe table ONCE, ahead of time, in your IaC or as a Phase 0 task (CREATE TABLE dr_write_probe(t timestamptz)) and replicate it like any other table — do not issue DDL against a Tier-0 ledger during an incident. On the day, the probe is an INSERT.
steps.command:
aws rds describe-global-clusters --global-cluster-identifier <id> --region <recovery-region> --query "GlobalClusters[0].GlobalClusterMembers[].{arn:DBClusterArn,writer:IsWriter}"
# write probe (table pre-created ahead of time — see detail):
psql -h <recovery-writer-endpoint> -c "INSERT INTO dr_write_probe VALUES (now()); SELECT max(t) FROM dr_write_probe;"
# measured RPA:
psql -h <recovery-writer-endpoint> -c "SELECT now() - max(updated_at) AS staleness FROM <hot-table>"
steps.verify: IsWriter is true for the recovery-region cluster; the INSERT succeeds (the cluster accepts writes, it is not still read-only); staleness query returns a number you have written down
steps.pass: Writer is in the recovery region AND a write succeeds AND measured RPA is recorded. On the failover path, measured RPA must be inside the loss window approved in the PATH DECISION step — if it is worse, that is a finding and possibly a reason to hold.
steps.record: Per-database: operation performed (switchover|failover), new writer endpoint, write-probe result, measured RPA/loss window

steps.title: GATE: secrets resolve for the APPLICATION identity (before apps start)
steps.detail:
Placed between the data block and the compute block, because that is where it belongs: secrets are the #1 recovery killer, and apps started before their secrets resolve crash-loop with misleading application-shaped errors — you then spend RTA debugging L4 symptoms of an L3 cause. Hold the execution here on the plan's Manual approval block that sits between the data and compute blocks. If your plan has no such block you cannot gate an execution in flight: add one before this runbook is trusted, and until then run this check the moment the data block completes and be ready to cancel the execution.

Prove the WORKLOAD can obtain and USE each secret, not that a secret exists. get-secret-value returns the plaintext and therefore forces a KMS Decrypt; running it as the workload's own identity additionally proves the role policies, resource policies and — critically — the OIDC trust of a recovery-region EKS cluster whose issuer URL is DIFFERENT from the primary's. An admin's read proves none of that, and describe-secret proves less still: it returns metadata only and never touches KMS.

Three forms are given below in order of fidelity. Prefer exec'ing into the real workload; the probe pod bound to the same ServiceAccount is equivalent for identity; the secrets-init log check is the fallback when you can run neither, and it is the "app startup probe passes" form of the same evidence. If all you have is admin credentials, say so in the record and raise a finding — do not record an admin read as an app-identity read.
steps.command:
# Preferred: exec into the REAL workload — it already runs as the tier-0 identity.
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> exec deploy/<tier0-app> -- sh -c 'aws sts get-caller-identity && aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id <one-tier0-secret> --region <recovery-region> --query SecretString --output text >/dev/null && echo ok'
# Full sweep (use when the app image has no AWS CLI): mount the signed-off list into a
# probe pod bound to the SAME ServiceAccount, so the IRSA identity is identical.
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> create configmap dr-secret-list --from-file=signed-off-secrets.txt --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> apply -f -
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> run secret-probe --rm -i --restart=Never --image <recovery-registry>/aws-cli:<tag> --overrides='{"spec":{"serviceAccountName":"<tier0-serviceaccount>","containers":[{"name":"secret-probe","image":"<recovery-registry>/aws-cli:<tag>","volumeMounts":[{"name":"l","mountPath":"/l"}],"command":["sh","-c","aws sts get-caller-identity; while read s; do aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id \"$s\" --region <recovery-region> --query SecretString --output text >/dev/null && echo \"ok: $s\" || echo \"FAIL: $s\"; done </l/signed-off-secrets.txt"]}],"volumes":[{"name":"l","configMap":{"name":"dr-secret-list"}}]}}'
# Last resort if neither is possible: the app's own startup probe / secrets-init must pass.
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> logs -l app=<tier0-app> -c secrets-init --tail=50 | grep -iE 'error|notfound|accessdenied' && echo "SECRETS FAILING" || echo "secrets-init clean"
steps.verify: sts get-caller-identity returns the tier-0 IRSA ROLE (not the node instance role, not an admin); zero FAIL lines across the signed-off list; at least one successful get-secret-value per KMS key in play; secrets-init / startup probe logs clean
steps.pass: Every signed-off secret retrieved BY THE APPLICATION IDENTITY — this single command proves existence + KMS decrypt + IAM/OIDC trust together. Any FAIL line, or a caller identity that is not the app role, is a blocker: hold the execution and fix before the compute block runs.
steps.record: Caller identity returned; any failing secret (immediate blocker finding); KMS key ids exercised

steps.title: Block: compute scale-up (EKS / ASG / ECS)
steps.detail: The compute block scales recovery-region capacity from pilot-light to production size. Scaling blocks ask the region for capacity; they do not guarantee it — AWS recommends on-demand capacity reservations for critical applications, and insufficient-capacity errors during a real regional event (when every other tenant is scaling into the same region) are a known and likely failure. If you hit them, that is a HOLD decision for the incident commander, not something to retry silently: record it, because it is also the single most useful Phase 0 finding you can bring back.
steps.command:
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get nodes -o wide && kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get deploy -A -o wide
aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities --auto-scaling-group-name <asg> --region <recovery-region> --max-items 20 --query "Activities[].{s:StatusCode,d:StatusMessage}"
steps.verify: Node/task counts reach production targets; tier-0 workloads Ready; scaling activities show no InsufficientInstanceCapacity / limit errors
steps.pass: Compute block complete; tier-0 apps Ready at production capacity with zero capacity or quota errors (any capacity error is recorded even if a retry succeeded)
steps.record: Scale-up duration; every capacity/quota error verbatim; final node and replica counts

steps.title: GATE: image provenance — pods pull from the RECOVERY-region registry
steps.detail: This gate is new. A pod that pulls its image cross-region from the registry in the region you are evacuating passes the test and fails the disaster: it works today because the primary is only degraded, and it will not work when the primary is actually gone. Check the resolved image host on every running tier-0 pod, not the manifest in git.
steps.command:
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}' | sort -u
# and confirm nothing is still pulling: 
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> get events -A --field-selector reason=Failed | grep -i pull || true
steps.verify: Every image host is the recovery-region registry; zero image references containing the primary region; no ImagePullBackOff / Failed-pull events
steps.pass: Zero images referencing the primary region, on every tier-0 namespace. Any primary-region reference is a blocker finding even though the pod is Running.
steps.record: Distinct image hosts observed; any pod still referencing the primary region

steps.title: Block: custom Lambda actions (app-specific steps)
steps.detail: App-specific glue the orchestrator cannot know natively runs as Custom action Lambda execution blocks: warming caches, re-pointing region-bound config, enabling consumers, kicking batch schedulers in the NEW region only. CAUTION on the failover path: ungraceful mode SKIPS custom Lambda blocks and Lambda event-source-mapping blocks. Check your plan for which blocks were skipped and decide, for each, whether it was optional or whether you must now run it by hand — a must-run data action parked in a custom Lambda block is silently omitted exactly when you need it most.
steps.command:
aws arc-region-switch get-plan-execution --plan-arn <plan-arn> --execution-id <id> --region <recovery-region>
aws arc-region-switch list-plan-execution-events --plan-arn <plan-arn> --execution-id <id> --region <recovery-region>
steps.verify: Every custom action block reports success, OR is listed as skipped AND has an explicit decision recorded (ran by hand / not needed)
steps.pass: No failed custom blocks, and no skipped block left undecided
steps.record: Which custom actions ran, which were skipped by ungraceful mode, and the decision for each skip

steps.title: Verify edge, certificates and partner allowlists — WITHOUT touching public DNS
steps.detail: Prove the front door would work before you send anyone through it. Reach the recovery edge on its DIRECT endpoint with a Host header matching the real domain, so no public DNS changes. Confirm the certificate on the recovery edge is valid for the public domain (ACM certificates are REGIONAL — a valid cert in the primary region is worth nothing here, and a CloudFront cert must be in us-east-1). Confirm the partner and edge/WAF allowlists contain the recovery-region egress IPs, by asking the partner to confirm, not by assuming: an allowlist miss discovered after the cutover means partner traffic dies publicly, and it is the one thing you cannot fix during the event.
steps.command:
curl -sk https://<recovery-direct-endpoint>/healthz -H 'Host: api.<your-domain>' -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n'
openssl s_client -connect <recovery-edge>:443 -servername api.<your-domain> </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -subject
# from inside a recovered pod, prove outbound egress to the partner works:
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <tier0-ns> exec deploy/<tier0-app> -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' <partner-endpoint>/ping
steps.verify: HTTP 200 through the recovery edge via direct endpoint + Host header; certificate valid for the public domain and not near expiry; outbound call from a recovered pod reaches the partner; partner has confirmed the recovery egress IPs in writing
steps.pass: Edge path, certificate and partner allowlist all verified pre-cutover, with the partner's confirmation message captured
steps.record: Endpoint used, HTTP codes, cert dates and subject, partner confirmation message

steps.title: GATE: functional success bar BEFORE any traffic moves
steps.detail:
This is the step that used to come after the traffic flip, and moving it in front of the cutover is the single most important change in this runbook. L6 before L7: shifting live traffic onto a stack that has never completed a business transaction converts a regional outage into a customer-facing incident you caused. "Apps Ready at production capacity" is an L4 statement and it is not recovery.

Run the agreed business transaction end to end against the recovery region, through the direct endpoint with a Host header (still no public DNS change), and run the batch/settlement path too — batch paths fail differently from request paths. The first correct business response is T1; RTA = T1 - T0 (T0 = the approval in the APPROVAL GATE step).
steps.command:
curl -sk -X POST https://<recovery-direct-endpoint>/<business-tx-path> -H 'Host: api.<your-domain>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @test-transaction.json
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <ns> create job --from=cronjob/<settlement-import> dr-verify-import && kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <ns> logs -f job/dr-verify-import
steps.verify: Business-level success response carrying a real transaction id (a 200 with an error body is a FAIL); settlement/batch job completes and rows land in the recovered database
steps.pass: Both halves of the success bar pass in the recovery region before any traffic moves; T1 recorded. If this gate fails, DO NOT proceed to the traffic block — go to the rollback section.
steps.record: T1 timestamp; computed RTA; transaction id; batch job result and row counts

steps.title: APPROVAL GATE: authorize the live-traffic cutover
steps.detail: The plan's Manual approval execution block sits here, immediately before the traffic block, and this is the approval it is for. The decision-maker confirms out loud: the L6 bar passed (the L6 success-bar step), the edge/cert/allowlist checks passed (the L5 edge/cert/allowlist step), the old primary is fenced (the FENCE step), and the rollback owner can state the rollback from memory. Approving pauses nothing else; declining cancels the execution.
steps.command:
aws arc-region-switch approve-plan-execution-step \
  --plan-arn <plan-arn> --execution-id <id> --step-name <traffic-approval-step> \
  --approval approve --comment "L6 passed at <T1>; edge+cert+allowlist verified; primary fenced" \
  --region <recovery-region>
# to stop instead: same command with --approval decline (this cancels the execution)
steps.verify: Approval recorded against the execution step with the approver named; all four preconditions restated on the bridge
steps.pass: Explicit written GO from the named decision-maker, referencing the L6 evidence
steps.record: Approver, timestamp, the evidence cited

steps.title: Block: live-traffic cutover (Route 53 health check / ARC routing control)
steps.detail: The traffic block now flips live public traffic: Route 53 health-check state or an ARC routing control, both data-plane. This is L7, not L5 — it was previously mislabelled L5, which is how it ended up scheduled before the functional verification. Watch new connections arrive in the recovery region and old-region traffic decay over the TTL window. Verify from multiple resolvers, not just yours.
steps.command:
dig +short api.<your-domain> @1.1.1.1 && dig +short api.<your-domain> @8.8.8.8
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://api.<your-domain>/healthz
aws arc-region-switch get-plan-execution --plan-arn <plan-arn> --execution-id <id> --region <recovery-region>
steps.verify: Multiple public resolvers answer with recovery-region targets; real traffic arriving and succeeding in the recovery region; old-region request rate decaying
steps.pass: Live traffic served by the recovery region with error rate and latency inside normal bands
steps.record: Flip time; resolver answers; error-rate and latency observations both regions

steps.title: Prove the LIVE path with a real business transaction
steps.detail: The L6 gate proved the stack through the direct endpoint. This proves the public path: DNS, edge, WAF, allowlist, auth, app and data together. Ideally the partner sends it. A synthetic transaction through the public front door is the minimum.
steps.command: curl -s -X POST https://api.<your-domain>/<business-tx-path> -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @test-transaction.json
steps.verify: Correct business response via the PUBLIC domain; partner confirms on the bridge if they are in the loop
steps.pass: Live public business transaction answered correctly
steps.record: Transaction id; who sent it; timestamp

steps.title: Monitor the execution report to completion
steps.detail: Walk the full execution: every block green, every step duration logged, every warning read. A yellow or SKIPPED block is a finding even when traffic is flowing — especially on the failover path, where ungraceful mode skips blocks by design. Export the execution report (a PDF per execution delivered to S3) into the incident/test record. Region switch also measures recovery time itself (execution time plus time until the regional health alarms go green) — use that number and reconcile it against your own T1 rather than keeping two competing stopwatches.
steps.command:
aws arc-region-switch get-plan-execution --plan-arn <plan-arn> --execution-id <id> --region <recovery-region>
aws arc-region-switch list-plan-execution-events --plan-arn <plan-arn> --execution-id <id> --region <recovery-region>
steps.verify: Execution status COMPLETED; no failed steps; every skipped step has a recorded decision; report exported
steps.pass: Report saved into the record, with the skipped/warning list triaged
steps.record: Execution report link; Region switch's own measured recovery time vs your T1 - T0; skipped/warning list

steps.title: FAILOVER PATH ONLY: reconcile writes lost or stranded in the old region
steps.detail:
Skip this on the switchover path (RPO 0 — nothing was stranded). On the failover path, writes accepted by the old primary and not replicated before the failover are NOT in the new primary. They are not gone from the old region's storage, they are simply not in the ledger you are now serving from, and nobody will discover them for you.

With the reconciliation owner named in the APPROVAL GATE step: (1) once the old region is reachable, enumerate what it accepted after the last replicated transaction (use the old writer read-only — never re-open it for writes); (2) classify each record as MERGE (must be applied to the new primary, with idempotency and a conflict rule), REPLAY (re-derivable from a durable upstream source such as the event archive or the partner's own records), or DISCARD (accepted duplicate, or the loss window formally accepted); (3) apply the merges as a tracked data-fix change, not an ad-hoc psql session; (4) record counts for every class. Also decide what happens to the old region's message backlog when it returns: purge, drain to a quarantine queue for review, or process idempotently with a staleness check — hours-old messages arriving into a moved-on database is the failure people forget.

If you cannot enumerate the stranded writes, say so in the record and name what the business should tell customers. Silence here is how a data-loss event becomes a data-integrity event.
steps.command:
# read-only enumeration against the OLD writer once reachable (do not re-enable writes):
psql -h <old-writer-endpoint> -c "SELECT * FROM <ledger> WHERE updated_at > '<last-replicated-timestamp>' ORDER BY updated_at"
steps.verify: Stranded-write set enumerated (or explicitly declared un-enumerable); every record classified merge/replay/discard; merges applied through a tracked change; counts recorded
steps.pass: Reconciliation record signed by the named owner with counts per class and any customer-facing consequence stated. "We accepted the loss" is a valid outcome ONLY when written down with a number.
steps.record: Last replicated transaction timestamp; counts merged/replayed/discarded; ticket for the data fix; message-backlog decision

steps.title: Communications: stakeholders and partners
steps.detail: Announce completion to the incident channel, exec sponsor and affected partners (they may see new egress IPs, brief errors, or a settlement file arriving from a different source). Keep the status page honest, and on the failover path say plainly that a bounded data-loss window occurred and is being reconciled — partners discovering that themselves is far more expensive than being told.
steps.verify: Comms sent per the comms plan; partner acknowledgements received; status page reflects reality including any data-loss window
steps.pass: All notified parties acknowledged
steps.record: Who was notified, when, and what was said about data loss

rollback.title: MID-FLIGHT: hold, continue, or reverse — and who decides
rollback.detail:
Read this the moment a block fails, because "we finished, now reverse" is not the shape of a bad failover. Establish which side is authoritative for WRITES right now, then choose:

A. Nothing promoted yet (failure at or before the FENCE / start-execution steps, data block not complete): the old primary is still the writer. REVERSE is cheap — cancel the execution, unfence the old region (restore SG ingress, scale workloads back, re-enable schedulers), confirm the old writer accepts writes, and stand down. Nothing needs reconciling.

B. Data promoted, compute or edge failed (this is the most likely bad case): the RECOVERY region is now authoritative for writes and the old primary is demoted or fenced. Do NOT reverse by reflex — reversing means a second promotion, and if any writes have landed in the recovery region they will be stranded by it. Default to HOLD: keep the recovery region as the write side, keep public traffic where it is (it has not moved yet — the traffic block is last for exactly this reason), fix forward on compute/edge, and re-run the L6 gate. Only reverse if the recovery region cannot be made to work at all, and then treat it as a full planned switchover back, with its own fence, its own verification and its own reconciliation step.

C. Traffic moved and the live path is failing: go to the emergency rollback below.

The decision is the incident commander's, not the operator's, and it is recorded with the time and the reason. Cancelling an execution is cancel-plan-execution; declining a manual-approval step also cancels it.
rollback.command:
aws arc-region-switch get-plan-execution --plan-arn <plan-arn> --execution-id <id> --region <recovery-region>
# state A only — unfence the old primary:
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id <db-sg> --protocol tcp --port 5432 --source-group <app-sg> --region <primary-region>
rollback.verify: Which side is authoritative for writes is established and written down; state A/B/C named; decision (hold|continue|reverse) recorded with the decider and the time
rollback.pass: A named decision in the record before any further action. Proceeding without naming the state is how a bad failover becomes a data-integrity incident.
rollback.record: Authoritative write side; state A/B/C; decision; decider; time

rollback.title: EMERGENCY (traffic already moved): quiesce → verify → move traffic back
rollback.detail:
Only for state C: traffic has been cut over and the live path is failing. Do NOT flip DNS back first. The old primary is fenced or demoted by the FENCE step, so routing live writes at it produces a second, self-inflicted outage — and every write taken in the recovery region since the cutover would be orphaned.

Order: (1) QUIESCE — stop accepting new writes at the recovery edge (maintenance response / drain), so the write set stops growing while you decide; (2) establish the write path you are moving traffic TO, and prove it: reverse the switchover so the old region is writer again (this is a second switchover, with the same risks, and it requires the recovery region to be healthy enough to sync), then run a write probe against the old writer and confirm it succeeds; (3) ONLY THEN move traffic back; (4) re-run the business transaction against the primary; (5) reconcile everything written in the recovery region between the cutover and the quiesce — that set is small and knowable if you quiesced promptly, and unknowable if you flipped DNS first.

What is NOT safely reversible, and you must know this BEFORE you plan a rollback around it:
  - An ungraceful Aurora failover cannot be un-done. You can only promote the other side again, which is another lossy event unless both sides are healthy and synced.
  - After an ungraceful failover the OLD cluster is typically detached from the global database. Re-adding it means rebuilding the secondary and waiting for a full resync — hours for a large volume, not minutes. So on the failover path, "reverse the promotion" is usually NOT available inside any patience window: plan to go forward, not back.
  - Writes accepted in the recovery region are never returned to the old primary by reversing DNS or by reversing the switchover. They come back only through the reconciliation step, by hand.
  - Side effects that already fired do not reverse either: rotated credentials, partner-side config changes, schema migrations, sent notifications. Check which custom actions ran.

If the recovery region is so broken that step (2) cannot complete, you are in a dual-degraded state: keep traffic where the data is authoritative, declare a customer-facing incident, and escalate — do not move traffic to a region that cannot take writes in order to make a dashboard look better.
rollback.command:
# 1. quiesce at the recovery edge (stop the write set growing)
# 2. reverse the data primary, then PROVE the write path before moving traffic:
aws rds switchover-global-cluster --global-cluster-identifier <id> --target-db-cluster-identifier <original-cluster-arn> --region <recovery-region>
psql -h <original-writer-endpoint> -c "INSERT INTO dr_write_probe VALUES (now()); SELECT max(t) FROM dr_write_probe;"
# 3. only now move traffic back
aws arc-region-switch start-plan-execution --plan-arn <plan-arn> --target-region <primary-region> --action activate --mode graceful --comment "rollback of <execution-id>" --region <primary-region>
rollback.verify: Writes quiesced at the recovery edge; the original region is writer again AND a write probe succeeds against it BEFORE any DNS/routing change; after the move, the business transaction succeeds via the public domain
rollback.pass: Traffic is only moved after the destination has demonstrably accepted a write; business transaction succeeds in the original region; the set of writes taken in the recovery region during the exercise is captured for reconciliation
rollback.record: Quiesce time; reverse-switchover result; write-probe output; traffic-move time; the captured recovery-region write set (with a reconciliation ticket)

rollback.title: Re-establish replication before considering any failback
rollback.detail: After a successful failover you are running single-region with no DR. Re-arm replication toward the original region and confirm lag is seconds, not hours, before anyone schedules a return trip. Region switch's post-recovery workflow (--action postRecovery, which needs the recovery execution id and both regions healthy) exists for exactly this.
rollback.command:
aws rds describe-global-clusters --global-cluster-identifier <id> --region <recovery-region>
aws arc-region-switch start-plan-execution --plan-arn <plan-arn> --target-region <primary-region> --action postRecovery --recovery-execution-id <recovery-execution-id> --region <recovery-region>
rollback.verify: Replication streaming from the new primary back to the original region; lag measured in seconds; DR posture restored and stated
rollback.pass: Both regions in sync and a written statement of current DR posture (which region is primary, what the RPO is now)
rollback.record: Lag numbers; post-recovery execution id; current DR posture

rollback.title: Decide failback as its own planned operation — not today
rollback.detail: Failing back is a SECOND switchover with the same risks and the same reconciliation obligations. Do not fail back on the day of the event unless forced. When the original region is proven healthy and replication lag is near zero, schedule the return as its own planned graceful execution, in its own window, with its own approval, its own fence of the (now) old primary, its own L6-before-L7 ordering, and its own reconciliation step. Run this same runbook in the other direction; the symmetry is the point.
rollback.verify: Written failback decision with a date, an owner, and the preconditions it waits on
rollback.pass: Decision recorded; failback scheduled as a planned graceful execution or explicitly deferred with a reason

templates.notes: Rehearsal: there is NO practice or simulation mode for Region switch — scheduled "practice runs" are an ARC zonal-autoshift feature, a different capability. You rehearse by EXECUTING the plan in graceful mode against a lower environment, at least quarterly, which is exactly your Phase-1 recovery-test loop for L1-L6. Plan evaluation runs automatically every ~30 minutes and AWS states explicitly that it is not a substitute for executing the plan; treat its warnings as a Phase 0 input. CLI surface verified 2026-09-16: start-plan-execution takes required --plan-arn, --target-region and --action (activate|deactivate|postRecovery) plus optional --mode (graceful|ungraceful, default graceful); approve-plan-execution-step takes --approval (approve|decline); cancel-plan-execution is the abort path. Sources: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/arc-region-switch/latest/api/API_StartPlanExecution.html , https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/arc-region-switch/start-plan-execution.html , https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/arc-region-switch/approve-plan-execution-step.html , https://docs.aws.amazon.com/r53recovery/latest/dg/region-switch-plans.html , https://docs.aws.amazon.com/r53recovery/latest/dg/manual-approval-block.html . Ordering note for the plan itself: the Route 53 health-check block and the ARC routing-control block BOTH move live public traffic, so both are L7 and both belong after a Manual approval block that follows your L6 verification. Estimated minutes are a planning estimate, not a schedule — you advance on gates, never on timers.

templates.description: Failover for stacks whose control plane (git + CI + IaC state) lives OUTSIDE the blast radius: fence the old primary, flip a single primary_region variable in git, apply, let reconciliation waves converge, promote data, verify parity, cut DNS. Rollback is the same flip reversed.
templates.whenToUse: Use when infrastructure is fully declarative (Terraform/Flux/Argo) and the deploy control plane demonstrably survives the primary region's loss. If CI or state storage lives in the failing region, fix that first — this runbook assumes it.
templates.name: Regional failover — GitOps primary_region flip
preconditions: Control plane (git host, CI runners, IaC state) confirmed healthy and outside the failing region
Both regions' stacks were green at last reconciliation
primary_region variable is the SINGLE switch — no hidden region-bound literals (verified by grep in CI)
Data replication (e.g. Aurora Global) healthy with low lag

steps.title: Preflight: both regions green in the deploy system
steps.detail: Check the CD dashboard: last reconciliation of BOTH region stacks succeeded. Failing over on top of a red recovery-region stack converts one incident into two.
steps.command: flux get kustomizations --context <recovery-ctx> # placeholder
steps.verify: Recovery-region stack reconciled and healthy; drift zero
steps.pass: Green in both regions (or documented known-red accepted by approver)
steps.record: Reconciliation timestamps both regions — approval here is T0

steps.title: Fence the old primary: disable writers (avoid split-brain)
steps.detail: Before promoting anything, make sure the old primary CANNOT accept writes even if it flickers back: scale writers to zero via the old region's stack if reachable, revoke DB security-group ingress, or disable the old writer endpoint. Split-brain is the one failure worse than downtime.
steps.command: kubectl --context <primary-ctx> scale deploy -n <ns> --all --replicas=0 # placeholder; if region unreachable, revoke SG ingress instead
steps.verify: No write traffic reaching old-primary database (connections drop to zero)
steps.pass: Old primary fenced or confirmed unreachable
steps.record: Fencing method used and evidence

steps.title: Flip primary_region in git
steps.detail: One commit: change primary_region from the failing region to the recovery region in the environment's variables file. PR with emergency approval per the incident process; merge. The commit SHA is your audit trail.
steps.command: git commit -am 'DR: primary_region <primary> -> <recovery>' && git push # via PR
steps.verify: Merged to the environment branch; CI pipeline triggered
steps.pass: Flip commit merged, pipeline running
steps.record: Commit SHA, PR link, approver

steps.title: Apply and watch reconciliation waves converge
steps.detail: Terraform apply / Flux-Argo reconciliation now reshapes the recovery region into 'primary' (scale-ups, feature flags, schedulers on). Waves converge in dependency order — watch each wave, do not intervene manually unless a wave is truly stuck (manual edits create drift you'll pay for later).
steps.command: terraform apply -auto-approve tfplan # placeholder / flux reconcile ks --with-source
steps.verify: All applies/reconciliations complete without error; no perpetual-diff loops
steps.pass: Recovery region converged to primary configuration
steps.record: Apply duration per stack; anything applied out-of-band

steps.title: Promote data: managed database switchover
steps.detail: Promote the recovery-region database to writer (Aurora Global switchover if the old primary is alive — zero loss; failover if it is not — bounded loss, record the window). Update nothing by hand that the IaC already points at via region-neutral endpoints.
steps.command: aws rds switchover-global-cluster --global-cluster-identifier <id> --target-db-cluster-identifier <recovery-cluster-arn> # placeholder
steps.verify: Writer endpoint now in recovery region; apps connect via the neutral endpoint
steps.pass: Writes succeeding in recovery region; no app pointing at old writer
steps.record: Switchover vs failover; data-loss window if any

steps.title: Run the parity/verification suite
steps.detail: Run the automated parity suite against the new primary: health endpoints, a synthetic business transaction, queue consumers draining, cron/batch schedulers active exactly once (in the NEW region only — double-running batch jobs is a classic split-brain leftover).
steps.command: ./scripts/dr-parity-suite.sh --target <recovery-region> # placeholder
steps.verify: Suite green: business tx OK, consumers draining, schedulers single-region
steps.pass: Parity suite passes; first business success is T1
steps.record: Suite output; T1; RTA = T1 − T0

steps.title: Cut over DNS
steps.detail: Flip public DNS (alias/weighted records) to the recovery-region edge. With health-check-based records this may already have happened — verify rather than assume.
steps.command: aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id <zone> --change-batch file://flip.json # placeholder
steps.verify: dig answers recovery-region targets; real traffic arriving and succeeding
steps.pass: Live traffic served by new primary
steps.record: DNS change time; TTL observed

rollback.title: Rollback = the same flip, reversed
rollback.detail: The symmetry is the point: when the original region is healthy again, fence current writers, flip primary_region back in git, apply, promote data back, run the parity suite, cut DNS. Same runbook, opposite direction, in a planned window with its own approval.
rollback.verify: Same gates as failover, in reverse
rollback.pass: Parity suite green in original region; traffic cut back

templates.notes: The single-variable flip is only as real as your last grep for region-bound literals. Keep a CI check that fails on hardcoded regions.

templates.templateName: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) — EC2 workloads
templates.description: Failover for EC2/VM-based workloads using AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery: continuous block-level replication, drill vs recovery launches, right-sizing on launch, and reverse replication for failback.
templates.whenToUse: Use for lift-and-shift / EC2-based (or on-prem source) servers protected by AWS DRS. Not for containerized or managed-service stacks — those belong to the snapshot-tool or orchestrated runbooks.
templates.name: Failover — Elastic Disaster Recovery (EC2)
preconditions: All source servers show Healthy replication in the DRS console
Launch templates reviewed (subnet, SG, instance type) in the last month
Most recent drill completed successfully and instance right-sizing validated
IAM permissions for launch verified in the recovery region

steps.title: Verify replication health and lag
steps.detail: In the DRS console (recovery region), confirm every source server is CONTINUOUS with lag near zero and no stalled data. Lag now is data loss later — record it as your expected RPA.
steps.command: aws drs describe-source-servers --region <recovery-region> --query 'items[].{id:sourceServerID,state:dataReplicationInfo.dataReplicationState,lag:dataReplicationInfo.lagDuration}' # placeholder
steps.verify: All servers CONTINUOUS; lag under the RPO target
steps.pass: Replication healthy across the fleet
steps.record: Lag per server — expected RPA. Launch decision time is T0

steps.title: Choose launch type: DRILL vs RECOVERY
steps.detail: Drill launches are isolated and safe to run anytime; recovery launches are the real thing. Confirm with the approver which this is — the console buttons are adjacent and the difference is an outage report.
steps.verify: Written confirmation of drill vs recovery from approver
steps.pass: Launch type confirmed and recorded
steps.record: Launch type + approver

steps.title: Launch recovery instances from latest point-in-time
steps.detail: Launch all servers (batch by dependency tier: data servers first, then app, then front-end) from the latest — or a chosen consistent — point in time.
steps.command: aws drs start-recovery --source-servers sourceServerID=<id1> sourceServerID=<id2> --is-drill <true|false> # placeholder
steps.verify: Recovery job running; instances entering 'launched' state
steps.pass: All instances launched without job errors
steps.record: Job id; per-server launch result

steps.title: Verify instance right-sizing and boot health
steps.detail: Check launched instance types against expected sizing (DRS right-sizing can pick a different family), OS boot success via instance screenshots/SSM, and disk mounts. An instance that boots but under-sized will fall over at real load.
steps.command: aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=tag:AWSDRS,Values=* --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType,State.Name]' # placeholder
steps.verify: SSM reachable on every instance; types match sizing sheet
steps.pass: All instances healthy and correctly sized
steps.record: Any sizing deviations

steps.title: Verify data volumes and application data freshness
steps.detail: On database/stateful servers: volumes mounted, services started, latest-transaction timestamps compared to T0 → measured RPA.
steps.command: ssm start-session --target <db-instance> # then check service + freshness query
steps.verify: Data services up; freshness within replication-lag expectations
steps.pass: Data layer verified; RPA recorded
steps.record: Measured RPA per data server

steps.title: Start applications and verify service health
steps.detail: Start app services in dependency order, verify inter-server connectivity (SGs in the recovery VPC), and health endpoints.
steps.command: curl -s http://<internal-lb>/healthz # placeholder
steps.verify: All app health checks green
steps.pass: Application tier healthy
steps.record: Services requiring manual intervention

steps.title: Business transaction verification
steps.detail: Run the agreed business transaction against the recovered fleet (direct endpoint in a drill; through the real front door in a genuine failover). First success = T1.
steps.command: curl -s -X POST http://<endpoint>/<business-tx-path> -d @test-transaction.json # placeholder
steps.verify: Business-level success response
steps.pass: Success bar met; T1 and RTA recorded
steps.record: T1; RTA = T1 − T0

steps.title: Drill only: terminate drill instances
steps.detail: For drills, terminate recovery instances via DRS (not raw EC2 terminate — let DRS clean up its jobs) once findings are captured. Replication continues untouched.
steps.command: aws drs terminate-recovery-instances --recovery-instance-ids <ids> # placeholder
steps.verify: Drill instances gone; source servers still CONTINUOUS
steps.pass: Clean teardown, replication unaffected
steps.record: Teardown time

rollback.title: Failback: reverse replication to original region
rollback.detail: After a real failover, start reversed replication (recovery instances become sources). Wait for CONTINUOUS with near-zero lag before scheduling failback.
rollback.verify: Reversed replication CONTINUOUS for all servers

rollback.title: Failback launch and traffic cutback
rollback.detail: In a planned window: quiesce writes, launch in the original region from the reversed replication, verify the business transaction, then cut DNS back. Same discipline as the failover.
rollback.verify: Business transaction succeeds in original region; DNS cut back
rollback.pass: Failback complete; replication re-reversed toward recovery region

templates.notes: DRS drills are cheap and isolated — run them monthly. The dangerous moments are launch-type selection and failback.

templates.description: The live exercise that wraps any failover runbook: real DNS flip, real partner transaction, real rollback plan, in a scheduled window with comms open and a decision-maker present. This is where RTO claims become real.
templates.whenToUse: Only after at least one clean Phase-1 recovery test. Use to exercise L7 (live cutover) with partners in the loop, inside an announced maintenance window, with a rehearsed rollback.
templates.name: Game day — live regional failover exercise
preconditions: A Phase-1 recovery test has passed cleanly within the last quarter

The underlying failover runbook's data path is CONTINUOUS replication with promotion (Aurora Global switchover/failover, DRS, ElastiCache Global Datastore...). Snapshot/point-in-time recovery tooling is Phase 1 only and must NOT take live traffic — see the underlying-runbook step, which lists which runbooks are eligible.
Maintenance window scheduled and announced to customers/partners
Partner has a named engineer on the bridge with a test transaction ready
Recovery-region egress IPs added to partner/edge allowlists IN ADVANCE
Rollback rehearsed on paper by the people who will execute it — including which branch (A or B) applies, because a game day that promotes data has a different rollback from one that does not
A data-reconciliation owner is named for writes taken in the recovery region during the exercise, BEFORE the window opens

steps.title: Open the bridge and comms channels
steps.detail: Open the incident bridge and the announcement channel at window start. Roll call: operator, approver/decision-maker, partner engineer, comms lead. No role present, no game day.
steps.verify: All named roles confirmed on the bridge
steps.pass: Roll call complete; window officially open
steps.record: Attendee list; window start time

steps.title: Go/no-go: preflight, rollback readiness, and which rollback branch applies
steps.detail:
Walk the morning-of preflight checklist aloud. The decision-maker gives an explicit GO recorded in the decision log. Confirm the rollback steps are printed/open and the person executing rollback can state them from memory.

New and non-negotiable: state OUT LOUD which rollback branch this exercise is on, because they are not interchangeable.

BRANCH A — read-only exercise: no data primary is promoted; the primary region keeps taking all writes; the recovery region serves reads only. DNS-first rollback is safe and fast here.

BRANCH B — data promoted: the underlying runbook promotes a data primary and/or fences the old one, so the RECOVERY region becomes authoritative for writes. DNS-first rollback is DANGEROUS here and the rollback sequence is quiesce -> reverse -> verify the write path -> then move traffic, with a reconciliation step after. Most game days worth running are Branch B.

Write the branch in the record before GO. An operator under time pressure will read the rollback section and nothing else; the branch is what makes it correct.
steps.verify: Preflight green; rollback owner recites the rollback plan; branch A or B named in the decision log; reconciliation owner named (branch B)
steps.pass: GO recorded with the branch and the reconciliation owner — this is T0
steps.record: GO decision + T0 timestamp + rollback branch (A/B) + reconciliation owner

steps.title: Execute the underlying failover runbook (continuous-replication data paths only)
steps.detail:
Run the chosen failover runbook through its data/compute/app layers and its own L6 verification. This game-day runbook wraps it — keep both open; the game day adds the live-traffic edges around it.

WHICH RUNBOOKS ARE ELIGIBLE. Only runbooks whose data path is continuous replication with promotion: a Region switch plan (Aurora Global switchover/failover), a GitOps flip with a managed database switchover, DRS with continuous replication. A SNAPSHOT / point-in-time recovery environment must NOT take live traffic while the primary is still live and writing: it is by construction behind the primary by up to the recovery-point interval (~15 minutes for a typical snapshot tool), so real customer traffic on it means stale reads and divergent writes that then have to be merged back into a primary that never stopped. Snapshot tooling is Phase 1: direct endpoints, no DNS, no live traffic. If your only proven runbook is snapshot-based, the honest move is to keep doing Phase-1 tests and build a continuous-replication path before booking a game day.

Before leaving this step, write down the one fact the whole rollback depends on: WHICH SIDE IS NOW AUTHORITATIVE FOR WRITES, and whether the old primary has been fenced or demoted.
steps.verify: Underlying runbook complete through its own L6 verification; data path confirmed to be continuous replication (not a snapshot restore); authoritative write side recorded; fence state of the old primary recorded
steps.pass: Recovery stack verified end-to-end via DIRECT endpoints, and the record states plainly: writes are authoritative in <region>; old primary is <fenced|demoted|still writer>
steps.record: Which runbook, its own record link, authoritative write side, fence/demotion state of the old primary, promotion timestamp

steps.title: Confirm edge allowlists and certificates
steps.detail: Before flipping DNS: recovery egress IPs present in the partner's allowlist and the edge/WAF allowlist; certificate on the recovery edge valid for the public domain. Discovering an allowlist miss AFTER the flip means partner traffic dies publicly.
steps.command: openssl s_client -connect <recovery-edge>:443 -servername api.<your-domain> </dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates # placeholder
steps.verify: Partner confirms allowlist entries; cert valid
steps.pass: Edge path verified pre-flip
steps.record: Partner confirmation message

steps.title: DNS flip to recovery region
steps.detail: Flip the public records (or trip the routing control / health-check inversion). Announce 'flip executed' on the bridge. Watch TTL-driven propagation; old-region traffic should decay over the TTL window.
steps.command: aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id <zone> --change-batch file://flip.json # placeholder
steps.verify: dig from multiple resolvers answers recovery region
steps.pass: Public DNS answering recovery region
steps.record: Flip time; propagation notes

steps.title: Partner sends the LIVE test transaction
