steps.detail: The partner engineer sends the agreed live transaction through the production front door. This single transaction is the whole point of the day: it proves DNS, edge, allowlist, auth, app, data — everything — with real partner traffic.
steps.verify: Partner receives the correct business response and confirms on the bridge
steps.pass: Live partner transaction answered — this is T1
steps.record: T1; RTA = T1 − T0; partner's transaction id

steps.title: Soak: watch live traffic and error budgets
steps.detail:
Hold in the recovery region for the agreed soak period (e.g. 30-60 min). Watch error rates, latency, queue depths, settlement jobs. The decision-maker decides: extend, conclude, or roll back.

On branch B, remember what the soak is doing: it is accumulating real writes in the recovery region. Every minute of soak is a minute of data to reconcile later, and a longer soak makes the rollback slower, not safer. Note the wall-clock time writes started arriving — the reconciliation step needs that boundary. If you decide to roll back, go to the EMERGENCY rollback and read the branch you are on before touching DNS.
steps.verify: Error/latency within normal bands for the full soak
steps.pass: Soak clean; decision recorded
steps.record: Soak metrics summary; decision; first timestamp at which real writes arrived in the recovery region

steps.title: Planned return: quiesce, reverse the data primary, verify the write path, THEN move traffic
steps.detail:
Returning is a second failover, so it gets the same discipline as the first — and the order matters more here than anywhere else in the day, because by now there are real writes in the recovery region.

BRANCH A (nothing promoted): reverse the DNS/routing change, confirm the primary is serving, re-run the business transaction. Done.

BRANCH B (data promoted): (1) QUIESCE writes at the recovery edge so the write set stops growing and you know its boundary; (2) reverse the data promotion (a planned switchover back — it needs both sides healthy and synced, and it is a second promotion, not an undo); (3) PROVE the original region accepts a write with a write probe; (4) only now reverse the DNS/routing change; (5) re-run the business transaction through the public domain; (6) go to the reconciliation step below.

Never move traffic to a side you have not just proven accepts writes. That single rule is the difference between a game day and an outage you scheduled.
steps.command:
# BRANCH B sub-steps (2) and (3) from the detail above: reverse the promotion, then PROVE the write path
aws rds switchover-global-cluster --global-cluster-identifier <id> --target-db-cluster-identifier <original-cluster-arn> --region <recovery-region>
psql -h <original-writer-endpoint> -c "INSERT INTO dr_write_probe VALUES (now()); SELECT max(t) FROM dr_write_probe;"
# BRANCH B sub-step (4): only now reverse traffic
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id <zone> --change-batch file://flip-back.json
steps.verify: Branch B: quiesce time recorded; original region is writer again AND a write probe succeeded against it BEFORE the traffic change; after the change, dig answers primary and the partner transaction succeeds again
steps.pass: Traffic returned only after the destination demonstrably accepted a write; business transaction succeeds in the primary region; both regions back in their normal roles; the recovery-region write set is bounded and captured
steps.record: Quiesce time; reverse-promotion result; write-probe output; traffic-return time; first and last timestamp of writes taken in the recovery region

steps.title: BRANCH B ONLY: reconcile the writes taken in the recovery region during the exercise
steps.detail:
Skip on branch A (nothing was promoted, so nothing diverged). On branch B, every write accepted in the recovery region between the promotion (recorded in the underlying-runbook step) and the quiesce (recorded in the planned-return step) landed in a database that is no longer the primary. Reversing the switchover does not carry them home and neither does reversing DNS. Nobody will find them for you, and the people who notice first will be customers or the partner.

With the reconciliation owner named at GO:
1. BOUND the set. You have the promotion timestamp and the quiesce timestamp from the records above. Enumerate the rows written in that window in the recovery-region database, read-only.
2. CLASSIFY every record: MERGE (must be applied to the restored primary, with an idempotency key and a stated conflict rule), REPLAY (re-derivable from a durable upstream — the event archive, the partner's own records, an S3 landing zone), or DISCARD (synthetic exercise traffic, or a duplicate). Exercise traffic you generated yourself is usually DISCARD; anything a real customer or the partner sent is not.
3. APPLY the merges as a tracked data-fix change with a ticket and a reviewer — not an ad-hoc psql session at the end of a long day.
4. RECORD counts per class, and sign it off. "Zero records, exercise traffic only" is a perfectly good result; an empty section is not.
5. Decide the queue/stream backlog too: messages produced in the recovery region during the window, and messages that piled up in the primary region while it was fenced. Purge, quarantine for review, or reprocess idempotently with a staleness check — decide before you un-fence the consumers.

If you cannot bound or enumerate the set, say so explicitly and escalate: that is a finding about the exercise design (you lacked the timestamps or the query), and it is the most valuable thing the game day will teach you.
steps.command:
# bound the window using the promotion timestamp (underlying-runbook step) and the
# quiesce timestamp (planned-return step). READ-ONLY:
psql -h <recovery-writer-endpoint> -c "SELECT count(*), min(updated_at), max(updated_at) FROM <ledger> WHERE updated_at BETWEEN '<promotion-ts>' AND '<quiesce-ts>'"
psql -h <recovery-writer-endpoint> -c "SELECT * FROM <ledger> WHERE updated_at BETWEEN '<promotion-ts>' AND '<quiesce-ts>' ORDER BY updated_at"
steps.verify: Write window bounded by the two recorded timestamps; every record in it classified merge/replay/discard; merges applied through a tracked change; counts recorded and signed off by the named owner; queue/stream backlog decision recorded
steps.pass: A signed reconciliation record with counts per class (zero is a valid count, blank is not) and no unclassified records. Any record you cannot classify is a blocker finding.
steps.record: Promotion and quiesce timestamps; counts merged/replayed/discarded; data-fix ticket; backlog decision; owner signature

steps.title: Close: comms, decision log, same-day record
steps.detail: Announce window close to all audiences. File every decision made on the bridge into the decision log. Write the game-day record the same day — including the ugly parts — and schedule the retro within a week.
steps.verify: Record written; retro scheduled; findings filed as gaps/tickets
steps.pass: Window closed cleanly with full paper trail
steps.record: Record link; retro date

rollback.title: EMERGENCY rollback — FIRST establish which side is authoritative for writes
rollback.detail:
Read this before touching anything. Thirty seconds spent here is the difference between ending an incident and causing a worse one.

From the go/no-go step you know the branch; from the underlying-runbook step you know the authoritative write side and whether the old primary was fenced or demoted. Confirm it now rather than trusting memory:
- Which cluster is the writer? (describe the global cluster / check the writer endpoint.)
- Is the old primary reachable and writable, or fenced / demoted / read-only?
- Have real writes landed in the recovery region since the flip?

Then take EXACTLY ONE of the two branches below. Do not blend them.

BRANCH A (no data promoted, primary still the writer, nothing fenced): reversing DNS is safe and fast, and speed is the right call — go to "Branch A" below.

BRANCH B (data promoted and/or old primary fenced or demoted): reversing DNS FIRST would route live writes at a fenced or read-only database, turning a failing exercise into an outage you caused, and would orphan every write taken since the flip. Go to "Branch B" below.

If you genuinely cannot tell which branch you are on: assume B. B is slower and safe; A applied to a B situation is a customer-facing data incident.
rollback.command:
aws rds describe-global-clusters --global-cluster-identifier <id> --region <recovery-region> --query "GlobalClusters[0].GlobalClusterMembers[].{arn:DBClusterArn,writer:IsWriter}"
# is the ORIGINAL primary writable right now? (expect failure on branch B)
psql -h <original-writer-endpoint> -c "INSERT INTO dr_write_probe VALUES (now())" || echo "ORIGINAL PRIMARY IS NOT WRITABLE — YOU ARE ON BRANCH B"
rollback.verify: Writer side identified from the API (not from memory); writability of the original primary tested; branch A or B stated on the bridge
rollback.pass: Branch named out loud and written in the record before any traffic or database action
rollback.record: Writer cluster; original-primary writability result; branch chosen; time

rollback.title: BRANCH A rollback (nothing promoted): reverse the traffic change immediately
rollback.detail: Only when the branch-identification step above confirmed no data primary was promoted and nothing was fenced — the primary region is genuinely still healthy and still the writer. This is the case the original "DNS first, diagnose second" advice was written for, and here it is correct: if live traffic is failing after the flip and the fix is not obvious within the agreed patience window (e.g. 15 min), reverse the DNS/routing change first and diagnose afterwards. Announce it on the bridge; do not silently flip.
rollback.command:
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id <zone> --change-batch file://flip-back.json
dig +short api.<your-domain> @1.1.1.1 && curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://api.<your-domain>/healthz
rollback.verify: Public resolvers answer the primary region; partner confirms a successful transaction; error rate back to baseline
rollback.pass: Customer impact ended; exercise findings captured; no reconciliation needed (nothing was promoted)
rollback.record: What failed, patience-window decision, rollback time, confirmation that no data was promoted

rollback.title: BRANCH B rollback (data promoted): quiesce -> reverse -> verify writes -> THEN traffic
rollback.detail:
The primary is NOT still healthy in the sense that matters: the underlying-runbook step fenced or demoted it, so it cannot take writes. Flipping DNS back now would (1) point live writes at a fenced or read-only database — a second, self-inflicted outage — and (2) orphan every write taken in the recovery region since the flip.

In order, and announce each on the bridge:
1. QUIESCE writes at the recovery edge (maintenance response / drain / scale writers down). The site is already failing; stopping the write set from growing costs you nothing and bounds the reconciliation. Record the timestamp.
2. REVERSE the data promotion — a planned switchover back to the original region. This needs the recovery region healthy enough to sync; it is a second promotion, not an undo. IF THE UNDERLYING RUNBOOK DID AN UNGRACEFUL FAILOVER rather than a switchover, the old cluster is probably detached from the global database and reversing means a full rebuild and resync — hours, not minutes. In that case reversing is NOT available inside the patience window: stay in the recovery region, declare the incident, and fix forward. If the recovery region also cannot be made to work, STOP and escalate: you are dual-degraded and moving traffic will not fix it.
3. UNFENCE the original primary (restore DB security-group ingress, scale its workloads back, re-enable its schedulers) and PROVE IT: run a write probe and see it succeed.
4. ONLY NOW reverse the DNS/routing change.
5. Verify the business transaction through the public domain, with the partner if they are on the bridge.
6. Go to the reconciliation step (main steps) with your promotion and quiesce timestamps.

What is NOT safely reversible, state it plainly to the decision-maker: an ungraceful failover cannot be undone — you can only promote the other side again, which is another lossy event unless both sides are healthy and synced. Writes accepted in the recovery region are never returned automatically by reversing DNS or by reversing the switchover; they come back only through the reconciliation step, by hand. And if a rotation, migration or partner-side credential change fired during the exercise, reversing traffic does not reverse that either — check the custom actions that ran.

This branch is slower than the old "DNS first" advice. It is slower on purpose. The patience window applies to deciding, not to skipping steps.
rollback.command:
# 1. quiesce (example: stop the write path at the recovery edge)
kubectl --context <recovery-ctx> -n <ns> scale deploy <write-path-deploy> --replicas=0
# 2. reverse the promotion
aws rds switchover-global-cluster --global-cluster-identifier <id> --target-db-cluster-identifier <original-cluster-arn> --region <recovery-region>
# 3. unfence the original primary and PROVE it takes a write
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id <db-sg> --protocol tcp --port 5432 --source-group <app-sg> --region <primary-region>
psql -h <original-writer-endpoint> -c "INSERT INTO dr_write_probe VALUES (now()); SELECT max(t) FROM dr_write_probe;"
# 4. only now reverse traffic
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id <zone> --change-batch file://flip-back.json
rollback.verify: Quiesce timestamp recorded; original region is writer again; write probe against the original primary SUCCEEDS; only then do resolvers answer the primary; business transaction succeeds via the public domain
rollback.pass: Traffic moved only after the destination proved it accepts writes; customer impact ended; the recovery-region write window is bounded by two recorded timestamps and handed to the reconciliation owner
rollback.record: Quiesce time; reverse-switchover result; unfence actions; write-probe output; traffic-return time; write window handed off (with ticket)

templates.notes: A game day without a rehearsed rollback is a production incident you scheduled yourself — and a rollback that flips DNS back to a fenced or demoted primary IS that incident. The rollback here branches on one fact: was a data primary promoted? Establish it before you act (the first rollback step does exactly this), and if you cannot tell, assume it was. Two things this template deliberately refuses: snapshot/point-in-time recovery environments taking live traffic, and any traffic move to a side that has not just proven it accepts a write. Estimated minutes are a planning estimate, not a schedule.
